questions.q: Under Section 5(b) of the Banking Regulation Act 1949, 'banking' is defined as:
o: Only the business of lending money
Accepting, for the purpose of lending or investment, deposits of money from the public, repayable on demand or otherwise, and withdrawable by cheque, draft, order or otherwise
Only the business of currency printing
Only foreign exchange trading
questions.src: Banking Regulation Act 1949, Section 5(b) — statutory definition of 'banking' centred on accepting public deposits for lending/investment, repayable and withdrawable as specified

questions.q: The Banking Regulation Act, 1949 came into force with effect from:
o: 26 January 1950
16 March 1949
15 August 1947
1 April 1935
questions.src: Banking Regulation Act 1949 — came into effect from 16 March 1949, applies to the whole of India, consolidating the law relating to banking companies

questions.q: The fundamental legal relationship between a banker and a customer with a deposit account is generally characterised as:
o: Trustee and beneficiary in all respects
Primarily that of debtor and creditor (the bank owing the deposited sum to the customer), with additional specific duties (e.g., of secrecy, reasonable care) superimposed by law and banking practice
Principal and agent only, with no debtor-creditor element
Landlord and tenant
questions.src: Settled banking law principle — the core banker-customer relationship for a deposit account is debtor-creditor, with the bank owing the customer the deposited amount, layered with additional fiduciary-like duties (secrecy, care) recognised by courts and banking practice

questions.q: Under Section 13 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, a 'negotiable instrument' means a promissory note, bill of exchange, or cheque payable:
o: Only to a specifically named person, with no other mode of transfer permitted

Either to order or to bearer, and freely transferable by delivery or endorsement, giving the transferee good title even if the transferor's title was defective (subject to conditions for a holder in due course)
Only after court approval of each transfer
Only to government entities
questions.src: Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, Section 13 — defines negotiable instruments as payable to order or bearer, freely transferable; the concept of a 'holder in due course' obtaining good title despite defects in the transferor's title is central to negotiability

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three primary negotiable instruments specifically defined under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881?
o: Promissory Note
Bill of Exchange
Cheque
Fixed Deposit Receipt
questions.src: Negotiable Instruments Act 1881 — the three instruments the Act specifically defines and governs are the promissory note (Section 4), bill of exchange (Section 5), and cheque (Section 6); a Fixed Deposit Receipt is generally treated as non-negotiable and not covered by the Act in the same way

questions.q: Under Section 6 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (as amended), a 'cheque' is defined as a bill of exchange drawn on a specified banker, payable on demand, and includes:
o: Only a physical paper cheque, excluding all electronic forms
Both a paper cheque and 'the electronic image of a truncated cheque' and a cheque in the electronic form, reflecting modern banking practice
Only postal money orders
Only demand drafts issued abroad
questions.src: Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, Section 6 (as amended by the NI (Amendment) Act 2002) — extends 'cheque' to include truncated cheque images and electronic cheques, modernising the definition

questions.q: A 'Holder in Due Course' under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 refers to a person who has obtained possession of a negotiable instrument:
o: Through theft, with full knowledge of the theft

For consideration, before the amount became payable (before maturity), in good faith, and without sufficient cause to believe any defect existed in the title of the person from whom they derived title
Without paying anything for it
Only if they are a bank
questions.src: Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, Section 9 — defines 'holder in due course' as one who takes the instrument for consideration, in good faith, before maturity, and without notice of any defect in title; such a holder generally gets a title free from prior defects

questions.q: Under Section 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, until the contrary is proved, courts presume (among other things) that:
o: Every negotiable instrument was made/drawn/accepted/endorsed for consideration
No negotiable instrument was ever made for consideration
All cheques are automatically forged
Negotiable instruments never carry a presumption of any kind
questions.src: Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, Section 118 — statutory presumptions, including that every negotiable instrument was made/drawn for consideration, until the contrary is proved; this presumption is central to Section 138 cheque-bounce prosecutions

questions.q: Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, dishonour of a cheque due to insufficiency of funds (where all statutory conditions are met) is punishable with:
o: Imprisonment up to 6 months only, with no fine option
Imprisonment up to 2 years, or a fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or both
A mandatory fine of exactly ₹10,000, with no imprisonment possible
Life imprisonment
questions.src: Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, Section 138 — punishment of imprisonment up to 2 years, or fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both; verified as unchanged across multiple independent 2025-2026 sources

questions.q: Under Section 138, after a cheque is dishonoured, the payee must issue a written demand notice to the drawer within how many days of receiving information (from the bank) about the dishonour?
o: 7 days
15 days
30 days
60 days
questions.src: Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, Section 138 proviso (b) — demand notice must be issued within 30 days of receiving information of dishonour from the bank

questions.q: After receiving the Section 138 demand notice, the drawer has how many days to make payment before the payee's cause of action to file a complaint accrues?
o: 7 days
15 days
30 days
45 days
questions.src: Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, Section 138 proviso (c) — drawer has 15 days from receipt of notice to make payment; failure to pay within this period completes the cause of action

questions.q: An offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act is generally classified as:
o: Non-bailable, non-compoundable, cognizable
Bailable, compoundable, and non-cognizable — meaning parties can settle the matter at any stage under Section 147
Punishable only by death
Only triable by the High Court in the first instance
questions.src: Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, Section 147 — makes offences under the Act compoundable; Section 138 offences are bailable and non-cognizable, allowing settlement between parties at any stage

questions.q: Under Section 143A of the Negotiable Instruments Act (inserted by the NI (Amendment) Act, 2018), a court trying a Section 138 offence may direct the drawer to pay interim compensation to the complainant, up to what percentage of the cheque amount?
questions.src: Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, Section 143A (inserted by NI Amendment Act 2018) — court may direct interim compensation up to 20% of the cheque amount, a significant reform addressing delays faced by genuine payees

questions.q: Under Section 148 of the Negotiable Instruments Act (also inserted by the 2018 Amendment), when an appeal is filed by the convicted drawer against a Section 138 conviction, the Appellate Court may direct the appellant to deposit a minimum of what percentage of the fine/compensation awarded by the trial court, pending appeal?
questions.src: Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, Section 148 (inserted by NI Amendment Act 2018) — Appellate Court may direct deposit of a minimum of 20% of the fine/compensation as a condition for suspension of sentence pending appeal

questions.q: In a significant 2025 Supreme Court ruling on Section 138 demand notices, the Court held that if the amount demanded in the notice does not exactly match the cheque amount (e.g., due to added interest/penalty), the notice:
o: Remains fully valid regardless of any mismatch
Is rendered invalid, since strict compliance with the statutory requirement of demanding the cheque amount is mandatory
Is valid only if the mismatch favours the drawer
Has no legal significance either way
questions.src: Kaveri Plastics v. Mahdoom Bawa Bahrudeen Noorul (2025) — Supreme Court reaffirmed strict compliance: a demand notice that does not align exactly with the cheque amount is invalid

questions.q: 'Endorsement' of a negotiable instrument, under Section 15 of the NI Act, refers to:
o: The act of destroying the instrument
The signing of the instrument (generally on the back) by the maker/holder for the purpose of negotiation, transferring the right to the instrument to another person
Only the act of presenting the instrument for payment
A court order cancelling the instrument
questions.src: Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, Section 15 — endorsement is the signing of the instrument (usually on the back) for the purpose of negotiation, transferring rights

questions.q: 'Crossing' of a cheque (drawing two parallel transverse lines, with or without words like 'Account Payee') under Sections 123-131A of the NI Act primarily serves the purpose of:
o: Cancelling the cheque entirely
Directing that the cheque be paid only through a bank account (not paid in cash across the counter), thereby providing a safeguard against fraudulent encashment and creating a traceable paper trail
Doubling the cheque amount
Making the cheque payable to bearer instead of order
questions.src: Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, Sections 123-131A — crossing (general or special, with 'Account Payee' restrictions) ensures payment only through a bank account, a key fraud-prevention mechanism

questions.q: Under Section 87 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, a 'material alteration' made to a negotiable instrument without the consent of all parties liable on it generally has the effect of:
o: Having no legal consequence whatsoever
Rendering the instrument void as against any party who did not consent to the alteration (subject to specific exceptions like alterations apparent and consented to)
Automatically doubling the instrument's value
Making the instrument non-transferable only
questions.src: Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, Section 87 — material alteration without consent of all liable parties voids the instrument as against non-consenting parties, subject to exceptions

questions.q: Under Section 85 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, a paying banker who makes payment on a cheque payable to order, in due course (i.e., in good faith and without negligence), is generally:
o: Always liable to the true owner if the endorsement later turns out to be forged
Discharged from liability, even if the endorsement of the payee/endorsee turns out to be forged, provided payment was made in due course
Never protected under any circumstances
Only protected if the cheque amount is below ₹5,000
questions.src: Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, Section 85 — statutory protection to the paying banker against forged endorsements, provided payment was made in due course (good faith, no negligence)

questions.q: Under Section 131 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, a banker who collects payment of a crossed cheque for a customer, in good faith and without negligence, is generally protected from liability to the true owner:
o: Under no circumstances whatsoever

Even if the customer's title to the cheque later turns out to be defective, provided the collection was made in good faith and without negligence, and the banker acted merely as an agent for collection
Only if the collecting bank is a nationalised bank
Only for cheques above ₹1 lakh
questions.src: Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, Section 131 — statutory protection for collecting bankers acting in good faith and without negligence, even where the customer's title was defective

questions.q: Among the recognised general duties a banker owes to a customer is the duty of secrecy/confidentiality regarding the customer's account. This duty is generally subject to well-recognised exceptions, including:
o: No exceptions exist under any circumstances

Disclosure compelled by law (e.g., under statute or court order), disclosure in the bank's own interest (e.g., recovery of dues), disclosure with the customer's express or implied consent, and disclosure per banking practice/usage
Only disclosure to family members of the customer
Only disclosure for marketing purposes
questions.src: Settled banking law principle (Tournier v. National Provincial and Union Bank of England, a foundational English case widely followed in India) — the duty of secrecy is qualified by recognised exceptions including legal compulsion, public duty, bank's interest, and customer consent

questions.q: A 'Banker's Lien' refers to the banker's general right to:
o: Seize any property of the customer located anywhere, without any connection to banking

Retain possession of securities, cash, or other property of the customer that comes into the bank's possession in its capacity as banker, as security for the customer's outstanding debts to the bank, until such debts are discharged
Automatically sell the customer's house without any legal process
Refuse to open any new account for the customer
questions.src: Settled banking law principle — a banker's lien is an implied pledge, allowing the bank to retain customer property/securities in its possession as banker as security against the customer's debts

questions.q: A banker's 'right of set-off' generally allows the bank to:
o: Never combine any accounts under any circumstances

Combine or adjust a customer's credit balance in one account against the customer's debit balance (an outstanding debt) in another account, subject to certain conditions (e.g., same customer, same right/capacity, no specific agreement to the contrary)
Only apply to accounts held in different banks
Only be exercised with a court order in every single instance
questions.src: Settled banking law principle — the right of set-off allows a bank to adjust a customer's debit balance in one account against a credit balance in another, subject to conditions of mutuality

questions.q: The SARFAESI Act, 2002 (Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act) primarily enables banks and financial institutions to:
o: Recover non-performing asset (NPA) dues by enforcing security interests (e.g., seizing and selling mortgaged/hypothecated assets) without first approaching a civil court, subject to specified procedural safeguards
Print additional currency for recovery purposes
Waive all outstanding loans automatically
Convert all secured loans into unsecured loans
questions.src: SARFAESI Act 2002 — enables secured creditors (banks/FIs) to enforce security interests and recover NPA dues without court intervention (subject to safeguards and borrower's right to approach the DRT), a major reform in debt recovery

questions.q: The Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT), established under the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act (RDB Act), primarily has jurisdiction to adjudicate:
o: Only criminal cases against bank employees

Applications by banks/financial institutions for recovery of debts due from borrowers above a specified pecuniary threshold, and appeals against actions taken by secured creditors under the SARFAESI Act
Only matrimonial disputes
Only disputes below ₹1,000
questions.src: Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act (RDB Act) — DRTs have jurisdiction over bank/FI debt recovery applications above the specified threshold, and hear appeals (as DRT/DRAT) against SARFAESI enforcement actions
